findings.rationale: The pilot had not completed a flight review in decades and his last medical application was denied in 2009, suggesting possible lapses in currency and qualification relevant to the accident.
The packet provides no description of the sequence of events or cause of the accident, so the cause cannot be determined from the facts given.
The airframe and engine logbooks were not located, indicating maintenance and inspection records may be absent, which could relate to airworthiness issues contributing to the accident.
Engine failed to restart and the propeller would not turn under starter, with a suspect right magneto and possible fuel degradation, pointing to an engine power-loss mechanism.
The right magneto failed to produce spark when rotated by hand, indicating an ignition system malfunction contributing to the loss of engine power.
Fuel onboard was possibly two years old after the airplane sat unflown for 26 months, suggesting fuel degradation as a possible contributor to engine power loss.
Maintenance records and the annual inspection completed the same day before the first flight raise a possible maintenance or inspection quality issue.
The pilot attempted a return to the departure airport at low altitude after an engine failure on a recently purchased airplane, suggesting planning or decision issues during the emergency.

The descent and turn toward a pond with groundspeed decreasing suggests a pilot decision or information processing issue such as fuel management or a forced-landing decision leading to loss of control or impact with water.
The fuel selector was found at about the 7 o'clock position and the fuel pump switch was off, suggesting improper use of fuel system equipment before impact.
The pilot was seriously injured and her husband wrote the account, but there is no evidence in the packet of incapacitation before the accident.
Pond water and mud were found in the fuel strainer bowl, indicating possible fuel contamination or fuel system issue, though the cause of the fuel selector position is unclear.
The cause of the loss of control and descent cannot be determined from the packet given the impact damage and the absence of a mechanical failure found in examination.
Angular wear on the left brake pad and disc with corroded, pitted anchor bolts points to a landing gear/brake assembly defect causing asymmetric braking and the leftward swerve on takeoff roll.
Corrosion of brake anchor bolts that should have been free of corrosion, despite a recent 100-hour inspection that replaced a left brake pad, suggests inadequate maintenance inspection.
The brake assembly was serviced during the December 2023 inspection yet retained corroded anchor bolts and an uneven pad wear pattern, suggesting a maintenance task performance lapse.
The student pilot's control inputs during the takeoff roll were likely inadequate to counter the left-drifting airplane, leading to a runway departure into the grass.

The accident occurred on a snow-covered 1,800-ft dirt private runway, and the airplane came to rest beyond the departure end, suggesting runway surface conditions may have affected the takeoff or landing roll.
The packet does not establish the departure time, the accident sequence, or the specific cause, as investigators could not determine the time of the accident or departure.
Winter conditions in the Colorado high-altitude area with snow cover suggest temperature and surface-related environmental factors may have contributed to the accident.
The flight was conducted from a short private dirt strip in winter conditions, and a decision to depart or continue on a marginal runway could represent an information processing or decision issue.
Engine controls-related malfunction is implicated since the compressor bleed-off valve was slow to close and the engine was shut down for troubleshooting during testing.
The power section showed buckling and internal rotational contact of the exhaust casing, indicating a turbine engine failure that led to the loss of power.
The bleed-off valve had been overhauled by an outside facility, and records show it was not installed at delivery, pointing to maintenance-related concerns with the valve assembly and part marking.
Two assembly part numbers were hand vibro-peened on the valve cover without strike-through, indicating a record or documentation irregularity in the overhaul.

The captain continued an unstabilized approach with a descent rate over 2,000 ft/min and chopped power to land rapidly despite the manual requiring a go-around, indicating an information processing and decision error.
The captain's actions, including abruptly chopping power and continuing the landing in poor conditions, reflect an inappropriate control action during the approach and landing.
Gusting wind and a roughly 15-knot tailwind on approach contributed to the excessive airspeed and high touchdown speed of 124 knots on a wet runway.
The runway surface was wet and the airplane hydroplaned after touchdown, reducing braking effectiveness.
The crew did not request a wind check or obtain updated weather, and the captain was distracted by requesting a different approach, indicating poor workload and task management.

Runway closure NOTAMs and the blocked runway were not effectively communicated to the arriving pilot, and the CTAF/air traffic information procedures for advising of the obstruction were ineffective, which relates to air traffic operating procedures.
The pilot did not hear the resident's repeated CTAF calls and the airport resident's handheld radio transmission range was limited to about 7-8 miles, pointing to a communication system deficiency.

Communication between the pilot and the CTAF/airport personnel failed to convey the runway obstruction, as the pilot did not acknowledge calls and airport staff did not coordinate a runway closure alert effectively.
The icy runway conditions contributed to the first airplane departing the runway and blocking the active runway that the accident airplane landed on.
The pilot's decision to continue a VFR approach into an airport with a known closure and limited communication, after cancelling IFR, reflects an information processing or decision issue.
The pilot failed to apply carburetor heat during troubleshooting in icing-conducive conditions, a information processing/decision error in response to the rough running engine.
Engine roughness in cruise with conditions conducive to serious carburetor icing points to a carburetor fuel/induction-related engine malfunction, with the pilot not applying carburetor heat.
The pilot chose to continue a high and fast approach and landed long rather than executing a go-around or extending the approach, an action error leading to the runway overrun.
Ambient temperature and dew point near 2°C and -2°C created conditions favorable to carburetor icing at cruise power.
The student pilot's limited experience in handling an emergency and high-energy approach may have contributed to the decisions made, though the packet provides little detail on this.

The fuel control unit control lever arm fractured from fatigue, preventing the FCU from achieving maximum fuel flow and causing the engine to lose power, which is an engine fuel and control system failure.
The engine would not accelerate past 45% Ng during the test run, indicating a power loss in the engine itself, though the root cause lies in the fuel control component.
The fuel system was involved only through the fuel control unit delivering insufficient fuel flow, so a broader fuel system finding is weakly supported.

The flight instructor and pilot receiving instruction appear to have mismanaged the flight, with the airplane departing controlled flight and spiraling after stall with no recovery, suggesting poor information processing or decision-making during an inadvertent stall/spin in an unfamiliar multi-engine airplane.

The pilot receiving instruction was in the front left seat with his hand on throttles and the instructor's hands were not on controls or engine levers, indicating a misuse or inadequate use of engine and flight controls during the critical phase.
Toxicology showed multiple CNS-depressant medications (alprazolam, zolpidem, amitriptyline, citalopram) in the flight instructor, which can impair mental state and judgment during flight.
Wind of 11 knots gusting to 23 knots and a SIGMET for turbulence from strong low-level winds were present, which likely contributed to the erratic flight and loss of control.
The pilot receiving instruction had only 9 hours in multi-engine airplanes and none in this make and model, suggesting inadequate multi-engine experience for the operation.

The pilot's decisions during the flight, including deflating the envelope with the rapid deflation system and continuing burner operation while the envelope collapsed, reflect poor information processing and decision-making under time pressure.

The pilot did not complete proper preflight planning and preparation: the flight was launched with an unsecured fuel cylinder, passengers walked under the tie-off rope, and the functional check of the deflation system was not evidenced.
The pilot's logbook had no entries since 2019 and the accident balloon was not logged, suggesting limited recent experience relevant to operating this balloon with skydiver exits.
Modification of the envelope with an unapproved swing rope that impacted the fabric likely compromised the envelope and contributed to the rapid deflation and collapse.
The pilot's persistent coughing and reported ketamine and medication presence suggest possible impairment or mental/physical state affecting his performance, though causation is uncertain.

The pilot continued into forecast icing and IMC without the required anti-icing equipment and did not heed controller warnings or low altitude alerts, indicating poor information processing and decision making about icing risk.

Forecast and observed conditions included moderate rime icing, freezing temperatures and supercooled large droplets in the cloud layer, which created the hazardous icing environment in which the airplane was flown.
The pilot lacked evidence of recent instrument proficiency and had a flight review entry with no year, indicating insufficient demonstrated qualification to fly IFR in IMC and icing.

The airplane was not equipped with operable anti-icing or de-icing systems for known icing, as no such equipment was found in the wreckage and the service bulletin placarded flight in known icing as prohibited.

The pilot's failure to respond to repeated controller calls and his unexplained 10-minute descent over a long track suggest possible incapacitation or a mental state issue, though the cause remains undetermined.

Night IMC conditions with low ceiling and mist over water suggest the pilot likely continued VFR-type flight into instrument conditions, a decision/information-processing failure leading to loss of control over the bay.
Broken ceiling at 300 ft, mist, and reduced visibility at night over the Pacific coast created instrument conditions that the pilot encountered during the flight.
Spatial disorientation is a typical consequence of night flight in IMC over featureless water without visual horizon, consistent with the abrupt descent indicated by the engine sound and lights.
Trace ethanol detected in postmortem liver and spleen tissue is of uncertain significance given possible postmortem production, so impairment is only a weak possibility.
Fuel system anomalies were noted (loose fuel line B-nuts and fuel quantity discrepancy), but the evidence is inconclusive about any contribution to the accident.
Water contamination in the TBI regulator's air reference line and diaphragm disrupted fuel metering, pointing to an engine fuel and control malfunction causing the power loss.
The fuel delivery system modification, with the fuel regulator being the component affected by water, is a plausible fuel system contributor to the partial and total power loss.
The modified TBI installation and its air reference routing may reflect a maintenance or modification task performance issue, though the packet does not establish a specific error.

The right main landing gear brake system was maintained the day before and the airplane veered right with tire marks suggesting brake application, pointing to a possible landing gear/brake system malfunction or asymmetric braking issue.
The pilot applied brakes while engine power was applied and continued to veer right, suggesting a control or action error during the landing roll.

The mechanic performed maintenance on the right main gear brake system the day before the accident, suggesting a possible maintenance-related deficiency contributing to the asymmetric braking and directional control loss.
The airplane departed the right edge of the runway into deep gravel, indicating the runway edge surface may have contributed to the loss of directional control.

The landing gear system failed to extend normally, with the gear motor and pushrod/cable linkage to the main gear apparently binding, and the emergency extension lever was stiff, pointing to a landing gear system malfunction.
Fuel gauge readings were inaccurate and the left tank was found empty while the right still held fuel, indicating a fuel quantity indication/system problem contributing to the fuel situation.

The pilot spent about 40 minutes circling while diagnosing the gear problem and apparently relied on inaccurate fuel information, suggesting poor information processing or decision-making in managing the emergency.
Inaccurate fuel quantity gauge readings are an indicating system deficiency that misled the pilot about the remaining fuel.
Engine internal failure with No. 3 connecting rod separated from crankshaft, seized piston and crankcase hole is a turbine/reciprocating engine powerplant failure coded as engine failure.
Engine lubrication starvation (bearing heat distress on rod journals, connecting rod separation) points to the engine oil system failing to supply adequate lubrication, coded as engine oil system.
Logbooks lack the required 400-hour valve inspection, camshaft lobe inspection and SB 301B compliance, indicating maintenance task performance deficiencies.

The pilot continued operating with rising iron wear readings and oil additions, and the 2 and 4 quart additions were not acted on as the wear trend warranted, reflecting info processing/decision issues.
Maintenance records lack required entries for camshaft inspection, SB compliance and 400-hour inspections, and oil analysis follow-up was incomplete.

The borescope plug at port M was apparently not properly locked after maintenance performed on January 14, which points to a maintenance task performance error that allowed the port to be open and produce the fire.
The No. 2 engine experienced an internal fire that burned through the nacelle wall, indicating a power plant failure originating at the engine's combustor/diffuser area.
The work card was initialed by both technician and inspector, suggesting a possible oversight/inspection gap in verifying the locking feature was engaged.
Wildlife remains (cackling goose) were recovered from the cockpit, tail rotor area and pitch change links, indicating a bird strike with the helicopter in flight at low altitude.
The main rotor blades were fractured, the mast nut separated and the transmission separated from the fuselage, consistent with main rotor system failure following the bird strike.
Night light conditions and a 7 kt wind near 2323 local time could have limited the crew's ability to see and avoid birds at low altitude, though the evidence is limited.

The helicopter was flown at about 110 knots groundspeed at 500 to 600 ft AGL in an area of possible bird activity, exceeding the 80 knot guidance in the bulletin, which suggests a decision-related contributing factor.

Simultaneous loss of power in both engines with clean fuel and no carburetor malfunction points toward an engine fuel and induction delivery problem, such as carburetor icing or fuel delivery restriction, though the investigation did not confirm it.
The packet gives no determined probable cause; the engine power loss mechanism remains undetermined after testing and data review.
Temperature and humidity conditions favorable to carburetor icing in a light-aircraft carburetor system could explain simultaneous power loss, though this is speculative from the packet.

The crew chose not to deice or perform a tactile contamination check in snowing conditions with below-freezing temperatures, a decision-making error in evaluating ground icing risk and holdover limits.
Light snow and below-freezing conditions at IAD created a contamination environment that degraded wing lift and the aircraft's takeoff performance.
Neither pilot performed a tactile inspection of the lift-generating surfaces as required by the POH and operator procedures, a failure of the inspection task.
The aircraft flew with 20 degrees of flaps and decelerated near stall speed after takeoff, indicating a performance/control parameter mismatch from contamination-induced degradation.
The operator's guidance lacked a definition of active icing, which may have contributed to inadequate crew understanding of ground icing procedures.
Improperly secured brake caliper backplate retaining hardware on the brake system is an equipment/hardware defect that plausibly caused the left brake to fail and the airplane to veer right.
The pilot's response of releasing the brakes and applying full left rudder during the veer, rather than maintaining directional control, is an action error contributing to the runway excursion.
Improper retaining hardware on the brake calipers suggests a maintenance task performance error that left the brake assembly in an unsafe condition.
Brake system failure is a component malfunction, though the brake system is not strictly a fuel system; this code is weakly supported and likely not the best fit.
Soft dirt adjacent to the runway allowed the airplane to leave the runway and roll over the embankment, a contributing environmental factor to the severity of the excursion.

Cold oil thickening in the turbonormalizer wastegate control system and the flooded, fuel-rich engine start point to engine fuel and control malfunction or excessive fuel flow contributing to the power loss after takeoff.
The pilot took off without allowing the engine oil to warm and without a run-up, and continued the attempt after abnormal starting, reflecting poor action decisions.
The turbonormalizing system's boost control via oil-actuated wastegate and absolute controller was sensitive to cold oil, leading to overboost and loss of engine power in the departure climb.

The pilot's limited experience in the SR22 and turbocharged airplanes, with about 15 hours and no verified turbocharged logbook experience, likely reduced his ability to manage the cold-start and turbocharger system.

After engine loss in the departure climb the pilot apparently could not execute a safe response, and the impossible-turn profile into a right bank indicates a poor information processing or decision under emergency conditions.
The engine (reciprocating) suffered connecting rod and bearing failure with oil loss, pointing to a failure of the engine itself.
Catastrophic internal engine failure with a separated connecting rod and piston damage indicates a power plant failure as the primary mechanical cause.
The engine had not been overhauled in 34 years, suggesting inadequate maintenance or inspection of the powerplant as a contributing factor.
The left cockpit door separated in flight, creating a hole in the cockpit and disrupting the airplane, so an airframe door/hatch structural failure is a central factor.
The pilot reported checking the door latches before flight, and the door was found separated, which suggests a possible deficiency in the door latching or securing maintenance or preflight check.
Maintenance and inspection of the door latch and hatch mechanism may have been inadequate, since the door departed the airplane despite the pre-flight check.
The pilot's erratic flight, loss of control and final unusual attitude after the door departure and headset disruption point to an emotional or cognitive response to the emergency.
Night, moonlit but dark, unlit Everglades terrain with pilots reporting they could not see anything indicates limited visibility/darkness as a key environmental condition in the accident.

The airplane's descent occurred at night over an unlit area with limited external visual cues, consistent with spatial disorientation (somatogravic illusion) as described in the narrative's additional information and GIF angle analysis.

The left-seat pilot's night and instrument experience could not be determined and the right-seat pilot had only about 214 logged hours, suggesting limited experience for night instrument-type flight in these conditions.
Continuing the flight into dark, unlit terrain with degraded visual references and then a rapid descent suggests poor information processing or decision-making by the pilots.
Methamphetamine was detected in the left-seat pilot's blood and urine, which may have impaired judgment or perception, though the discrepant results and unclear impairment limit confidence.

Fuel pump voltage spikes, fuel supply restriction indications, and the simulated loss of fuel flow point to a fuel system problem (pump/fuel supply/blockage) as the initiating failure of the engine power loss.
Engine fuel and control: the fuel flow regulation via electrically driven pump voltage adjustment to maintain rotor rpm was disrupted, causing the rpm drops and engine power loss.

The collective limiter forced a descent and the UAS contacted the ground hard and re-climbed, with no height sensing to flare, reflecting a performance/control parameter limitation during partial power loss.
The pilot did not engage auto-land and maintained manual control during the landing after repeated fuel pump warnings, an information processing/decision issue relevant to the hard landing.
Possible contributing debris in the fuel system indicates a maintenance or fuel filtration deficiency, which the manufacturer addressed by modifying the fuel filtration.
The airplane penetrated a thunderstorm with heavy rain, hail and severe turbulence, so convective weather is the primary environmental factor in the damage.

The pilot elected to continue on a heading toward the storm gap rather than accepting the ATC offered northerly deviation, indicating a decision/information processing error in avoiding convective activity.
The pilot reported severe turbulence during the encounter, which contributed to the airframe damage.
The pilot's Garmin display lacked airborne radar and relied on delayed NEXRAD imagery with 3-5 minute latency, limiting effective use of weather information.
The crosswind and gusting wind (19-23 kts against a 20 kt limit) were the central environmental condition leading to the loss of directional control after touchdown on runway 36L.

The crew continued the approach with a calculated crosswind at or above the 20 kt limit and gust information not properly considered, reflecting poor information processing and decision-making about the wind data.
The PF relied on an incomplete and selectively checked ASOS picture (steady 13 kt wind, gusts ignored) rather than the full wind data, indicating misuse of available weather information.
Operational pressure to avoid a diversion to ORL and arrange passenger transportation likely influenced the decision to continue to MCO despite marginal crosswind conditions.
The PF's control inputs after touchdown (left aileron and ineffective right rudder) did not adequately counter the crosswind drift, leading the airplane off the runway surface.

The pilot's flight planning and fuel management were inadequate: the airplane flew about 4 hours on fuel with an endurance of about 3.75 hours, and the fuel stop decision was made on cost, indicating poor planning/preparation.

Information processing and decision-making were poor, as the pilot continued on a fuel-limited flight after an earlier low-fuel indication and then diverted for cheaper fuel, leaving insufficient reserves.
The total loss of engine power occurred during the maneuver with an empty gascolator and fuel tanks nearly dry, consistent with fuel exhaustion in the engine fuel system.
Workload management may have contributed while the solo pilot managed a multi-leg cross-country flight with a passenger animal and fuel issues, though support is limited.
Operating environment general, weak support; the diversion decisions are not clearly an external operating environment factor.

The pilot flew low over the tower and continued along the pipeline right-of-way into a 197-ft obstacle that was visible and marked, suggesting a failure to see and avoid or poor information processing and decision making.</rationale>
Failure to perceive and avoid the brightly marked tall tower during a low-altitude flight suggests inadequate attention or monitoring of the environment.</rationale>
Toxicology showed delta-8-THC, gabapentin and alprazolam, which can impair cognitive and psychomotor performance and judgment during flight.</rationale>
The unlit-to-aircraft obstacle, a 197-ft guyed MET tower with guy wires not on charts, was a contributing object hazard that the airplane struck during low flight.
The pilot's medical certificate had expired and he held only BasicMed, raising questions about qualifications and currency for this flight, though total experience was high.
The fuel selector valve was installed 180 degrees from correct orientation, so selector positions did not correspond to the intended tank feeds, a fuel system defect.

The pilot did not recognize the rough idle and incorrect fuel selector behavior during run-up and used the both position which was actually off, indicating an information processing or decision error.
Maintenance personnel apparently failed to correctly install or verify the fuel selector valve orientation, though the timing of the error is undetermined.
The pilot's use of the fuel selector and checklist during pretakeoff preparation did not detect the abnormal engine indication, indicating an equipment or information use shortfall.
Service bulletin SEB99-18 compliance was not documented in maintenance records, a possible record keeping gap contributing to undetected fuel system issues.

Pilot had documented TBI with neurocognitive deficits and toxicology showed THC, opioids, gabapentin, and trazodone, which may have impaired judgment and decision-making during the low-altitude maneuvering.
Toxicology detected multiple central nervous system depressants and psychoactive drugs (THC, codeine, gabapentin, trazodone, atomoxetine) that can cause impairment or incapacitation in flight.
The abrupt left bank and near-vertical descent after takeoff suggests a poor information-processing or decision response, consistent with impaired cognition from the pilot's TBI and drug effects.
The engine lost power during the climb and momentarily resumed, indicating a possible engine power loss, though the cause is not established in the packet.
The pilot had accumulated only 20 hours in 90 days and a checkride failure history, which may bear on proficiency for the accident maneuver.

The pilot's apparent decision to depart and turn back toward the runway at low altitude, with fuel management issues and possible impairment, suggests an information processing or decision error leading to loss of control.

Fuel quantity was not properly managed: the left wingtip tank was topped off while the fuel selector was left in an unsuitable position and fuel quantity appears inadequate for the flight, indicating improper use of fuel system information or equipment.
Toxicology showed sertraline, an SSRI with possible dizziness and drowsiness side effects, which may have contributed to impaired performance during the turnback.
Fueling and fuel selector management during departure may reflect workload or task management problems, though evidence is limited.
The loose common ground feed-through stud and missing lock washer/locking nut caused a loss of electrical power to the displays and engine systems, placing the fault in the electrical power system.
The ground stud was left without lock washer or locking nut and loosened, indicating a maintenance/assembly task performance lapse on the electrical connection.
The display system going blank was affected by the electrical ground fault, though the primary cause lies in the electrical power system rather than the equipment itself.
Carburetor icing risk and the fuel system/engine fuel and control arrangement are central to the narrative, as the engine ran normally on test but icing conditions were present in flight.
Model sounding indicates conditions conducive to serious carburetor icing at the flight altitudes, an environmental condition relevant to the engine power loss/accident sequence.

Pilot and passenger had limited recollection and the flight included an unplanned landing on a private airstrip at an unknown point, suggesting a decision/information processing issue in fuel and route management.
Fuel planning appears inadequate: departure with 36 gallons for a 216-minute flight at roughly 8 gph with limited reserve and the return trip requiring fuel the pilot may not have had.
The pilot did not complete a full preflight inspection, did not sample fuel, and did not use a checklist, indicating deficient task planning and preparation.
The pilot's decision to take off after a rushed, incomplete preflight without fuel sampling, despite water and debris found in the fuel, reflects poor information processing and decision making.
Water and debris contaminated the fuel in the right carburetor bowl and both fuel boost pump samples, which is consistent with a loss of power after takeoff from the right engine.
The pilot was in a hurry and displeased with the linemen's delay, which points to workload or time pressure affecting task performance.
Heavy recorded precipitation over the weeks the airplane sat outside likely allowed water into the fuel system, a condition that contributed to the contamination.

The pilot's response to the reported engine loss and fire, including the unplanned steep descent into a populated area rather than following the emergency checklist, suggests an information processing or decision error under stress.

The pilot did not follow the POH Engine Fire In Flight checklist (firewall air control, fuel selector off) or emergency descent procedure, indicating a use-of-equipment/information task performance issue.
The loose metered fuel hose b-nut at the metering valve outlet, about 1.25 flats from finger tight, points to a fuel delivery leak as a likely source of the in-flight fire and engine power loss.
The pilot had about 960 pilot-in-command hours, had never flown into CLW, and had difficulty locating the airport at night, suggesting limited experience with this operation.
Night conditions with an unlit or hard-to-find airport and the pilot's difficulty locating CLW contributed to the navigation and approach workload before the emergency.
Engine ran very rough in cruise with EGT drops across cylinders and no magneto-related fault found, suggesting an engine-internal or power plant problem in the engine itself.
The power plant as a whole lost power in cruise, leading to a forced off-airport-area landing; the power plant category captures the undetermined engine power loss.
The packet does not identify a specific cause for the rough running and the post-accident examination did not confirm a definitive failure mode.

Abrupt EGT decrease across multiple cylinders with stable fuel flow and pressure until the event points toward an engine fuel/induction-related delivery problem, though fuel system checks were normal.

The pilot's decision to take off and operate with both main wing tanks empty, relying on the fuselage tank only, is an information processing/decision error that likely led to fuel starvation and power loss.

Improper use of the fuel system and selector (running main tanks dry and not managing fuel quantity across tanks) is a task performance use-of-equipment error consistent with the fuel exhaustion sequence.

The fuel system was the mechanism of power loss: wing tanks empty and fuselage tank feed with the selector configuration produced interruption of fuel supply, though no mechanical malfunction was found.

The fuel selector was found between positions and not fully seated in detent, indicating the pilot's action in selecting fuel tank (fuel selector mismanagement) led to fuel starvation and engine power loss.
Improper use of the fuel selector equipment during the tank change, with the instructor not verifying selector position, fits use-of-equipment task performance errors.
The fuel system, specifically the fuel selector and tank supply, is central to the loss of engine power described in the narrative.
The student had limited experience in the accident airplane make and model (1.2 hours), which may have contributed to the fuel management error during training.
The flight instructor did not observe the fuel selector position during the tank change, suggesting an attention/monitoring lapse.
Engine rough running, rpm decrease, and internal failure debris (bearing material, rod end cap, piston rings) indicate an internal engine mechanical failure.
The Cessna 150 is reciprocating-engine powered and the failure involved rod end cap, piston rings and bearing material, pointing to the reciprocating engine itself.
Metallic debris found in the engine and oil tank but not in the oil screen or filter suggests a lubrication-related or oil system issue, though not confirmed.
Weather was VMC with good visibility and wind, so weather conditions do not appear to be a causal factor.

The crew conducted a high-altitude stall test in visible-moisture conditions with a known anti-ice concern, and their decision to proceed and not account for ice contamination risk reflects info processing/decision failure.

The crew planned and conducted a required post-maintenance stall test without adequate preparation for icing, weather conditions, and the stall identification system's characteristics, indicating planning/preparation deficiency.

The SIC had only a recent initial training with an unsatisfactory stall prevention rating initially, and the training did not include full stalls, suggesting training gaps relevant to the stall recovery.
Post-maintenance wing leading edge and de-icing panel reinstallation with leaks and a missing screw likely contaminated or degraded the wing's stall characteristics, reducing maximum lift.
The airframe fluid ice protection system was not activated before the stall test, and the wing leading edge de-icing system with leaking TKS lines is relevant to the degraded wing performance.

Both CF34-3B engines lost power during descent and deceleration, with HPC case corrosion causing variable geometry malfunction and compressor instability at sub-idle, pointing to an engine power-loss mechanism.
The variable geometry system (stator vane positioning controlled by the MFC and linkage) was degraded by corrosion in the spindle bores, producing off-schedule stator positions and slow VG response.
The operator's troubleshooting of the January 2024 hung starts followed a fault isolation tree where the VG pressure check (MP 68) was among the last items, a procedural issue in maintenance policy.
Saltwater exposure from the operator's coastal Florida base contributed to corrosion of the compressor case, an environmental substance effect on the engines.
Maintenance personnel did not identify the corrosion-related VG issue during hung-start troubleshooting, relevant to maintenance task performance.

The helicopter was operated at night in IMC/low ceilings with snow, rain and low visibility over mountainous desert, so adverse ceiling and visibility conditions contributed to the loss of outside visual references.}
Multiple altitude, airspeed and heading deviations near the end of flight are consistent with spatial disorientation after inadvertent entry into IMC at night without outside visual references.
The pilot chose to depart at night in deteriorating weather with an inoperative radar altimeter and inadequate instrument experience, reflecting poor info processing and go/no-go decision making.
The pilot had about 6.2 turbine hours, zero actual IMC experience and limited simulated IMC, which left him poorly qualified for instrument-condition flight.
The radar altimeter was inoperative or intermittent before departure, degrading the aircraft's terrain awareness systems during the night flight over terrain.
Mechanics improperly reconnected the brake hydraulic hoses and swapped wheel speed transducer connectors during the carbon brake installation, a maintenance task performance error.
The crossed hydraulic brake hoses to MLG brakes 3 and 4 caused reduced braking pressure and loss of braking on the right main gear, which is a hydraulic power/brake system defect.
The service bulletin tests and checks did not verify correct brake hydraulic line routing, suggesting a training or support/oversight gap in the maintenance procedure.
Brake system failure is primarily a hydraulic/brake system issue, but the taxonomy has no brake-specific code; the closest systems code for the braking hydraulics is the hydraulic power system.
The maintenance procedure as written (EO/SB) did not include verification steps that would detect crossed hydraulic lines or swapped transducers, indicating a policy/procedure deficiency.

The student and instructor continued the approach to the parallel runway after being cautioned about wake turbulence, indicating an information-processing or decision error in assessing the vortex hazard.

The flight instructor's training and the student's training on wake turbulence avoidance and recovery from induced roll appear to have been insufficient, as the aircraft was not kept above the larger aircraft's flightpath.
Wake turbulence from the preceding Boeing 757 on the adjacent parallel runway is an environmental/physical hazard that contributed to the aggressive roll of the light sport airplane.
The aircraft may have been affected by a perception or orientation issue during the close-in approach, though the evidence for this is limited.
Engine failure from crankshaft connecting rod and bearing failures with metal contamination throughout the oil system points to an engine internal mechanical failure.
Oil pressure dropped to near zero and bearing debris was found in the oil filter, screen, and sump, indicating an oil system related contribution to the bearing failure.
Engine operated well beyond the 2,000-hour TBO and the 12-year calendar limit with no recorded overhaul, suggesting an overhaul/maintenance policy issue.
Maintenance records show no overhaul despite the engine being built in 1980 and operating far past recommended overhaul intervals, indicating a maintenance task gap.
The pilot landed with the gear up, indicating a failure to properly process gear position information or make a correct landing-configuration decision before touchdown.
The landing gear switch was found in the down position after the accident, suggesting possible improper use of the gear selector or failure to verify gear configuration.
Gear-up landings typically reflect lapses in attention and monitoring of the gear configuration, especially shortly after takeoff in the traffic pattern.
The pilot elected to lose altitude by pushing the nose down on a high, fast approach instead of going around, a decision-making error that led to excess airspeed and runway overrun.
The flight was conducted with only about 2 quarts of oil despite the POH's required preflight oil check and a 5-quart minimum, indicating inadequate planning and preparation.
The pilot flew an unstabilized approach at roughly 88 knots landing speed versus the 75-knot POH final speed, an action-level error contributing to the overrun.
The airplane's airspeed and energy management on final were outside the POH performance parameters, producing a long landing distance and overrun.
The preflight oil quantity inspection was not properly performed given the very low oil level found after the event.
The left wing separated after impacting a tree, so the tree (an object in the physical environment) is a plausible causal element of the accident sequence.
The packet does not establish the cause of the tree impact or the flight circumstances, so the cause is best recorded as not determined.

The airplane struck a tree during the accident flight, suggesting a possible pilot information processing or decision error in maneuvering or terrain/obstacle avoidance, though the narrative does not establish the cause.

Weather was VMC with 10 sm visibility and light winds, so adverse ceiling or visibility is unlikely to be causal, but a low-confidence weather-related contribution cannot be excluded without further data.
The incident was caused by moderate to severe turbulence encountered in IMC during descent, which directly matches the turbulence condition category.

The crew relied on EFB turbulence products and weather radar that did not show the turbulence, and the flight continued into a forecast turbulence area, suggesting an information processing or decision issue regarding turbulence avoidance.
Cabin crew were conducting final compliance checks and securing galley equipment, and the seatbelt sign timing contributed to flight attendants being unseated, reflecting task demands during descent.
Controllers failed to relay the PIREP of moderate turbulence to the flight and the sector had poor PIREP dissemination, reflecting an oversight or procedural gap in the support of the flight.
The tail rotor driveshaft fractured, causing loss of tail rotor thrust, which points to a failure in the tail rotor drive system.
Loss of tail rotor thrust followed the driveshaft failure, so the tail rotor assembly is a secondary consideration, though its blades were undamaged.
The packet does not establish the root cause of the driveshaft fracture (e.g., fatigue, manufacturing, or maintenance), so the underlying cause remains undetermined.
The elevator control cable separated in flight, causing loss of elevator control, which is a flight control system failure.
Worn guard pins and rubbing damage suggest that maintenance or rigging of the elevator cable routing, including guard pin installation, was inadequate after the January 2023 cable replacement.
The elevator cable separated near the vertical stabilizer, so empennage-area structure or cable routing could be implicated, though the failure is primarily a control system component.
Maintenance logbook entries were reviewed postaccident, but no direct evidence shows a records deficiency contributed to the failure.
The airplane struck powerlines spanning the river, a wire-strike object hazard in the physical environment that directly caused the accident.
The pilot flew low over the river at high RPM into a known or visible powerline span, indicating poor information processing or decision-making regarding obstacle clearance.
Flying low over the river at low altitude without adequate planning for obstacle avoidance suggests a planning or preparation shortfall.
Pilot had hypertensive cardiovascular disease, and a cardiac event could not be excluded as a contributor, though the evidence was insufficient.
Fuel starvation symptoms on left tank selection and a fuel cap that failed to vent properly point to a fuel system (venting/supply) malfunction contributing to the loss of engine power.
The pilot continued unstabilized approaches at high speed with yawed attitude and multiple go-arounds, reflecting poor decision-making in managing the abnormal handling situation.

The rudder trim was found in the full nose-right position while the airplane tracked left and the pilot reported no rudder control, indicating a flight control (rudder trim/rudder) malfunction affected the approaches.

The pilot had only about 9 hours in make and model, no Cessna 182 entries in the logbook period, and limited recent experience, which may have contributed to the inability to control the airplane in the abnormal handling situation.

The pilot did not identify or correct the rudder trim setting and fuel selector issues during the familiarization and positioning flight, suggesting incomplete use of available equipment and information.

The alternator rotating magnet assembly slipped on the shaft due to a loose torque nut, a electrical power system anomaly that could have caused loss of electrical power and engine or avionics failure.
The modified automotive engine could have lost power in flight, though examination revealed no anomalies precluding normal operation.
The packet does not establish a definitive cause; examination found no conclusive preimpact anomaly beyond the alternator slip, so the cause may remain undetermined.
Ignition system was equipped with two independent systems that functioned properly, so ignition is unlikely the cause, though it was examined.
Pilot-induced or performance/control parameter issues at low altitude near dusk could be involved in a loss of control, but the packet provides insufficient evidence.
The loss of engine power resulted from a disconnected Pc line at the fuel control, a fuel control pneumatic/fuel regulation input failure within the engine fuel control system.
The B-nut on the Pc line lacked thread engagement after the 150/300-hour inspection, indicating a maintenance task performance deficiency during the February 2024 inspection.
The required inspection of B-nut torque paint alignment and security was apparently not properly performed or verified, reflecting an inspection task deficiency.
The manufacturer's special tool and CSL guidance for accessing the B-nut may indicate a training or support gap, though the evidence for this is weak.
Maintenance records show a multi-year gap with no documented condition inspections or storage preservation, indicating inadequate maintenance and inspection of the engine and airframe.
No maintenance entries show the engine storage preservation procedures were completed, indicating a maintenance task performance lapse by the owner or mechanic.
Engine power loss shortly after takeoff was caused by a seized No. 2 piston with internal corrosion on the cylinder wall and connecting rod, pointing to an engine internal failure.
Non-instrument-rated pilot flew VFR into IMC with heavy snow and an airplane in the clouds shortly after takeoff, a classic setup for spatial disorientation and loss of control.
The decision to depart into deteriorating snow and low visibility with icy conditions, despite a witness's concern, reflects poor information processing and go/no-go decision making.
Heavy snowfall and reduced visibility (about 1/2 mile, cloud at low altitude) were the environmental conditions that precluded visual flight.
The pilot was non-instrument-rated and had only about 20 hours of simulated instrument practice, indicating insufficient experience for flight in these conditions.
Diphenhydramine detected in toxicology may have caused sedation or impairment that could contribute to incapacitation or degraded performance.
Exhaust valve guide deposits and reduced stem-to-guide clearance indicate valve sticking in the engine's valve train, a power plant component failure mode central to the accident.
Lead, bromine and carbon deposits from fuel combustion and the SSP-525 reference to improper leaning point to an engine fuel and combustion management problem contributing to deposit formation.
Maintenance records show no valve or cylinder work since installation despite deposit buildup, suggesting inadequate maintenance or inspection of the valve guides.
Operating the engine with improper leaning and extended ground operation below normal temperature, as described in SSP-525, reflects pilot action contributing to sludge formation.

The loose fuel line from the throttle body to the fuel manifold leaking fuel points to an engine fuel and control system defect, consistent with the loss of power output and the fuel leak found at the metering throttle body.
The power plant as a whole was affected, as the pilot reported no change in power output and the engine would not start until the fuel line was tightened.
The fuel line was found looser than finger tight, which suggests an inadequate maintenance or assembly task performed before the flight.

The pilot under instruction flew a low approach while under a view-limiting device and did not recognize the low path until told to remove it, indicating faulty information processing and decision making during the approach.
Fuel quantity was not documented and the fuel selector was on the right tank, pointing to improper use of fuel quantity information and fuel system management before and during the approach.
Prior to departure there was no documentation of total fuel onboard, indicating inadequate flight planning and preparation regarding fuel quantity.
No evidence of fatigue or alertness issues is presented in the packet, so this is a weak candidate only.
Weather was VMC with light winds, so environmental conditions are unlikely to be a primary cause.

The pilot's final approach ended with the airplane low and to the left of centerline at about 50 ft, with flaps still up, suggesting a decision/information processing error in managing the approach and landing configuration rather than a mechanical failure.
Winds were gusting to 16-17 knots from roughly 120 degrees, a crosswind component relative to runway 5 that could have affected the low, left-of-centerline final approach.

The pilot's approach planning and configuration sequencing (flaps retained up near the ground, power at three-quarters) suggest inadequate planning or preparation for the landing at a short, constrained traffic pattern.
Managing a traffic pattern, flap configuration, and gusty winds at a low altitude over a short approach likely imposed a workload that could contribute to the loss of control near the ground.

The output bearing was not removed and repacked with fresh grease during the 300-hour maintenance task as the manual requires, and mechanics had not performed this step, pointing to a maintenance inspection and servicing deficiency.
Mechanics did not remove the output bearing for grease repack, and grease degradation with melted bearing components indicates the maintenance task was performed incompletely or improperly.
The overrunning clutch sits on the engine gearbox mounting pad and its output bearing failed thermally, making the accessory/gear drive assembly the most directly implicated component.

The failure chain originated in the engine-to-rotor drivetrain overrunning clutch assembly, which is an engine-side power transmission component, though the failure is mechanical rather than a control problem.

Mechanics appeared unclear on which inspection tasks they personally performed and whether the bearing removal was standard practice, suggesting a training or procedural knowledge gap at the operator.

Crankshaft bending, No. 2 main bearing wear and scoring, and witness reports of engine speed fluctuations and a momentary loss of engine noise suggest an in-flight reciprocating engine malfunction or power loss.
The fire damage, missing GPS memory chip, and untestable engine accessories leave the primary causal chain undetermined based on the packet alone.
The rapid, steep descent (about 5,300 ft/min) in daylight VMC toward a hill could reflect a spatial orientation or perception problem, though the record gives no direct evidence of one.
Engine ceased producing power in flight after fuel-related and lean-operation concerns, and the engine was reported shut down/sputtering, pointing to an engine power loss as a finding.

Fuel selector found between off and left main tank positions with ports not open, and fuel injector lines lacking fuel for three cylinders, indicating a fuel system delivery problem leading to the power loss.

The pilot continued at 2,500 ft past the landing point, declined to read back the clearance, and did not follow instructions to land, reflecting poor information processing and decision making during the approach.

The pilot's limited experience (about 200 hours with 18.5 night hours) in a night arrival over 180 miles suggests inadequate flight planning and preparation for the night approach and fuel management.
Low total time and limited night experience suggest insufficient experience/qualifications for the complex night IFR-like arrival and emergency handling.
Crankshaft fatigue cracking in the engine led to the loss of engine power and the forced landing, so the engine (reciprocating) failure is the primary mechanical cause.
The failure occurred in the reciprocating engine itself (TSIO-550 crankshaft and cylinder barrel damage), which fits the engine reciprocating category.
General power plant category covers the engine failure at a broad level when the specific component is not further attributable.
Maintenance-related operational capability is not clearly supported since no recent crankshaft maintenance was found and fatigue life was the issue.
The left aileron direct cable separated in flight, causing loss of aileron control, which is a flight control system failure.
Maintenance failed to detect and correct corrosion, broken strands, and pulley binding during inspections and the cable replacement, and cable material was changed without anti-corrosion treatment.
Maintenance personnel did not routinely apply anti-corrosion products to galvanized steel aileron cables, a maintenance task performance shortfall.
Corrosion of several structural tubes and the landing gear was found, indicating airframe structural deterioration in the fuselage.
Maintenance personnel may not have been adequately trained on corrosion-prevention and cable inspection requirements given the Piper Note 24 wipe-down procedure apparently was not followed.
Maintenance personnel reinstalled the T-bolt with attachment bolts finger-tight and never torqued or safety wired them, and the removal was undocumented, a clear maintenance task performance error.

The aircraft maintenance and inspection process failed to detect the missing T-bolt and unsecured attachment hardware before release to service, reflecting a maintenance/inspection deficiency on the aircraft.
