The pilot made a steep left turn at low altitude shortly after takeoff following engine installation, a decision-making/information processing error consistent with a low-altitude turn-back or stall/spin scenario.
The pilot's documented mental illness, medication and wife's concern about his mental state suggest a psychological/emotional state factor that may have affected his actions.
Sedating medications including diphenhydramine and gabapentin were detected at high levels, which can cause impairment and incapacitation affecting the pilot's control of the aircraft.
The steep bank at low altitude near stall speed, with stall speed rising in a turn, indicates a performance/control parameter exceedance leading to an inadvertent stall and loss of control.
Weather was VMC with good visibility, so weather is unlikely to be a causal factor and this is included only at low confidence as a general environmental placeholder.
The pilot failed to apply carburetor heat during conditions favorable to serious icing, which is an information processing and decision error about recognizing icing risk.

Engine power loss in a carbureted Cessna 172 under serious carburetor icing conditions points to the engine fuel and control system (carburetor) as the mechanism of power loss, since all other engine components checked normal.
Ambient temperature near 80°F with a 71°F dew point created an environment conducive to carburetor icing at high humidity.

The captain's decision-making about runway condition (believing runway was dry despite RCAM 3/3/3 and FO perceiving wet, plus disabling autobrakes and delaying manual braking) reflects info processing/decision errors.
Crew actions were inadequate: autobrakes were disarmed early, manual braking was delayed and under-applied, and the aircraft was not slowed before turning off a wet runway at high speed.

Landing planning and preparation were deficient: the crew requested a runway change and roll-to-end approval, and reduced autobrake setting despite the FM requirement for autobrake 3 or max with RCAM 3/3/3 or less.
Possible knowledge or training gap regarding wet runway braking procedures, speedbrake timing, and autobrake/manual braking effectiveness, though training was recent and current.
Instrument meteorological conditions and reduced visibility on approach may have contributed to the perception of runway surface, though visibility under the clouds was reported as good.
The pilot continued flight into deteriorating IMC and descending toward terrain while attempting to divert, indicating poor information processing and go/no-go decision making.
Night IMC with heavy rain and lowering ceilings and reduced visibility created conditions that made visual terrain avoidance and controlled flight difficult.
Blood ethanol impairment from alcohol consumed before the flight, with open and unopened cans recovered, indicates pilot impairment affecting performance.
The pilot had an argument with his wife and left home after drinking, suggesting a mental/emotional state that impaired judgment before the flight.
The pilot's experience in instrument conditions at night appears limited given the flight into IMC and loss of control near terrain, though the packet does not establish his qualifications.
Engine lost power during climb with rapid fuel flow decrease and water found in the fuel flow manifold, pointing to a fuel delivery/engine fuel and control problem.
Fuel system contamination with water is indicated by the positive SAR-GEL test and the empty airframe fuel strainer, implicating the fuel system.
Engine power loss could alternatively stem from internal engine failure, though the rotational continuity and compression on all cylinders weaken this.

The crew failed to cross-check or verify the altimeter setting and did not conduct an approach briefing, and the flight continued unstabilized into terrain, reflecting poor information processing and decision making during the approach.

The PIC had documented repeated FMS and approach-procedure weaknesses in training and was passed through checkrides despite instructor recommendations that he needed more training, pointing to training and qualification deficiencies.
The crew did not understand the FLOC mode on the FMS, and the autopilot/flight guidance mode confusion during the approach reflects misuse of equipment and information.

Crew attention was divided during the approach as the PIC could not see the airport until late and the autopilot state was unclear, with the glideslope deviations and descent going unnoticed until the go-around call.
Very strong winds of 19 to 38 knots with known downdrafts on approach to runway 25 and mountain wave activity likely contributed to the unstabilized descent below the glideslope.

The pilot had about 788 total hours, only 12 in the prior 30 days, no instrument training logged, and the flight entered icing and IMC-forecast conditions with a climb to 13,300 ft and a descending turn, suggesting poor information processing or decision-making about continuing into hazardous weather.
Limited recent experience and no logged instrument flight time suggest the pilot's qualifications were insufficient for flight in forecast icing, mountain obscuration and IFR conditions.
G-AIRMET forecast IFR conditions and mountain obscuration over the accident area, which would reduce ceiling and visibility and could have contributed to loss of control or terrain impact.
Forecast and pilot-reported icing conditions with SLD probability at the accident altitude indicate icing as an environmental factor affecting the airplane's performance and controllability.
The sharp groundspeed decay followed by a descending right turn at altitude may reflect inadequate attention to or monitoring of the aircraft's energy state and surroundings.

The fluids (FR-200 and MVP-Fx retardants, particularly comingled mixtures with low pH and galvanic pitting) are the direct source of the widespread corrosion and residue buildup in the tanks, structure, and engines.
Corrosion of primary structure such as the right-wing forward spar lower cap doubler on Tanker 106 is a significant structural degradation finding.

The design/qualification process for the new retardant and tank materials did not adequately evaluate galvanic and comingling compatibility with aircraft alloys, a development-stage organizational shortcoming.

Retardant (a corrosive chemical substance) contacting and corroding airframe and engine materials is the environmental agent in this event, though the taxonomy code fits the substance mainly as an external hazard category rather than a precise cause.
Oversight of the field evaluation allowed comingling of incompatible retardants on operational airtankers despite earlier recommendations against it.

The pilot's decision-making and information processing during the electrical failure, including apparently failing to reset generators and mishandling the checklist, is central to the loss of electrical power and gear-related landing damage.

Pilot's training and knowledge gaps on King Air electrical system, generator reset procedures, and absence of an electrical failure checklist suggest inadequate training on emergency electrical procedures.
The electrical power system failed with the generators offline, with generator caution light bulbs broken and a battery with degraded capacity, indicating an electrical system malfunction.
The main landing gear buckled on touchdown after the manual extension, with gear down-and-locked not verifiable due to loss of power, implicating the landing gear system in the damage.
The pilot's use of the emergency landing gear extension and electrical checklists appears to have been improper or incomplete, pointing to misuse of procedures and information.

Engine lost total power after fuel flow and fuel pressure dropped to zero simultaneously, pointing to an engine fuel delivery/control malfunction such as the fuel pump or fuel metering system failing to supply fuel.

The fuel system (tank selection, supply, and pump components) is implicated because fuel pressure and flow both dropped to zero, though the examined plumbing and pumps were found unobstructed and operational.
The specific reason for the fuel flow and pressure loss and the low No. 3 cylinder EGT was not determined from the postaccident examination, which found no obstructions or governor defects.

The pilot's abrupt, unannounced-to-passenger transfer of control ('my airplane') followed by an unstable, fast approach and turn toward the runway suggests a control or action error during the approach.
The pilot's last logged flight was in 2015 and he held no instructor rating, so his recent experience in this weight-shift aircraft while instructing a passenger was likely inadequate.
The instructional flight plan focused on repeated takeoffs and landings with a passenger after a long local flight, which may reflect inadequate task planning or workload management in the approach.
Wind speed was unknown in the packet, and wind-related gusts or drift over the right side of the runway could have contributed to the drift and fast approach, though this is unconfirmed.

The left main landing gear retract rod assembly fractured in ductile overstress and buckled, causing the left main gear to fail to extend and requiring a gear-up landing, which is a landing gear system failure.

The most recent annual inspection recorded no defects despite the retract rod's corrosion and rub marks, suggesting the required inspection of linkages for wear and distortion was not adequately performed.
The retract rod punctured the gearbox case, indicating structural damage to the gear actuation housing, though the primary failure was in the linkage rather than the nacelle structure.
The precise reason the retract rod overstressed and buckled, including the role of the primer rub and sliding contact, is not fully determined from the packet.

The annual inspection did not identify the linkage wear or distortion that the Appendix D checklist requires inspecting, suggesting inadequate inspection guidance or training support for linkage components.
Engine oil system failure leading to oil starvation (loss of oil pressure, connecting rod overheating, large oil loss) points to an engine oil system fault as the mechanism of the accident.

The engine suffered catastrophic internal failure (seized crankshaft, failed connecting rods, crankcase breach) consistent with a turbine/reciprocating engine internal failure following oil starvation.
Possible maintenance-related oil system deficiency such as improper oil servicing or sealing, though the evidence for a maintenance lapse is not conclusive from the packet.
The specific initiating cause of the oil loss was not determined from the packet, as the source of oil loss could not be identified.

The engine suffered a catastrophic internal failure with a fractured crankcase and connecting rod, indicating an engine (reciprocating) component failure as the mechanical cause of the forced landing.
The failure involved the reciprocating engine's connecting rod and piston pin bushings, so the reciprocating engine itself is the implicated power plant component.
The mechanic did not follow the critical service bulletin for connecting rod bushing inspection, a maintenance and inspection lapse that allowed the worn bushings to go undetected.
The mechanic's maintenance task performance deviated from the manufacturer's mandatory inspection procedures by not following CSB07-01A, and the metal in the filter was not escalated appropriately.
Possible shortfall in training or knowledge of the mechanic regarding the service bulletin, though the packet does not establish this directly.

The pilot chose to continue a landing in deteriorating weather with precipitation and gusty winds, then applied full power after touchdown, indicating a decision-making error in managing the landing with insufficient runway remaining.

Visibility dropped to 1.75 statute miles in moderate rain with a broken ceiling at 800 feet, and the pilot was operating in IMC-like conditions near a precipitation area, which contributed to the hazardous landing environment.
Gusting winds up to 14 knots with variable direction between 220 and 320 degrees during the approach likely affected landing control and alignment with runway 6.
The pilot was managing a weather-related approach while dealing with multiple approach requests and ATC advisories about precipitation, which may have increased workload during the landing phase.

The airplane left the paved runway surface and traveled over grass, then dropped off the airport into a ravine, indicating the runway end and terrain beyond the departure end contributed to the accident outcome.
A discolored scat tube near the header pipe indicates exhaust heat exposure and a likely exhaust system leak or overheating that ignited smoke and fire in the cockpit area.
Engine-related heat/smoke event with engine noise change points to a power plant or engine problem as the initiating condition.
The pilot returned to the airport after smelling smoke, then reattached a damaged scat tube with a zip tie and redeparted without adequate corrective maintenance, a decision-making issue.
Field repair of the discolored scat tube with a zip tie instead of proper inspection and replacement reflects a maintenance task performance deficiency.
Improper securing of a cooling/scat tube with a zip tie to an engine mount near hot exhaust can allow contact or fire spread into the fuselage area.
The fuel injector servo idle mixture was found set excessively rich, a fuel-metering engine fuel control defect causing the overboost/rich condition.
The annual inspection in December 2023 left the idle mixture and fuel pressure incorrectly set, indicating a maintenance task performance error.
Maintenance-manual and SIL guidance on idle mixture adjustment was not adequately followed or effective, pointing to a policy/procedure deficiency in the maintenance process.
The pilot continued operating with the overboost warning and manually leaned the mixture rather than resolving the abnormal condition, reflecting info processing/decision issues.
The turbocharger installation with fixed exhaust bypass may contribute to manifold pressure and overboost issues, though the evidence is limited.

The pilot continued trimming near encroaching tree limbs and was assessing whether the tree line could be trimmed safely, suggesting an information processing or decision error about obstacle clearance during the low-level work.
Tree limbs and branches were the object contacted during the descent, and the wreckage shows crush damage from trees, indicating object strike in the operating environment as a causal factor.

Tree trimming with an external saw in mountainous terrain at the end of a full day of flights may have imposed high task demands on the pilot, which could contribute to the decision to work close to the tree line.
The ignition coil produced no spark during hand rotation with the ignition switched on, indicating an ignition system failure as a likely cause of the power loss.
Total engine power loss after power reduction with failed restart, and a fuel stop just before the event, suggests a possible engine fuel and control issue, though the investigation points elsewhere.
The pilot's restart attempt with choke and fuel pump on and his decision to perform a forced landing in a field may reflect action choices contributing to the damage.
Student pilot personnel issues are not clearly established, though inexperience could be relevant to the power loss handling; confidence is low.
The fuel injector regulator was contaminated with fuel/oil, which likely degraded fuel metering and caused the sluggish engine power loss during takeoff.

The engine failed to produce normal rpm and power during takeoff, indicating a powerplant performance deficiency, though the crankshaft and valvetrain were continuous and no internal engine failure was found.

The manufacturer service bulletin on servo-equipped injectors with updraft mounting recommended inspection for contamination that was not evidently performed, suggesting a maintenance inspection shortfall.
The magnetos were found with timing advanced to 28 degrees BTDC versus the specified 25 degrees, a possible contributing deviation to reduced power output.

The pilot believed the engine stopped producing power after takeoff, and the carburetor-equipped engine with fuel recovered from bowls points to an engine fuel and control issue, though the examination found no clear fault.
Temperature of 75.2°F with dew point 62.6°F and about 65% relative humidity is conducive to carburetor icing, which can cause loss of engine power in a carbureted engine.
The pilot's delayed recognition and response to the power loss shortly after takeoff may reflect information processing or decision issues, though the packet provides limited evidence.

The pilot elected to return to land with an open door and then descended steeply at low altitude in the traffic pattern, suggesting a poor information processing or decision during the return, with the door distraction likely contributing.

The airplane was flown at low altitude and reduced airspeed in the pattern, then entered a steep nose-down descent with a roll, consistent with an aerodynamic stall from performance/control parameters being exceeded.

The pilot was dealing with an in-flight door opening shortly after takeoff while maneuvering in the pattern, a workload-intensive situation consistent with task saturation leading to loss of airspeed and control.
The pilot had only one landing in the prior 90 days and a prior fatal-adjacent accident in 2023 involving a stall, indicating limited recent experience and qualifications for the flight.

The carburetor heat control cable was loose and not secured to the attachment bolt, and the heat door had limited travel, pointing to a fuel/induction control malfunction that prevented full carburetor heat operation and contributed to the loss of power.

Maintenance records show a logbook entry on carburetor heat control travel shortly before the accident, and the loose unsecured cable suggests improper maintenance or inspection of the carburetor heat control linkage.
The improperly secured cable and absent safety wire suggest a maintenance task performance error in reinstalling or adjusting the carburetor heat control.

The DPE and applicant did not identify the carburetor heat control malfunction during the simulated emergency and go-around, indicating a decision or information processing shortfall in diagnosing the power loss.
Carburetor icing or fuel delivery issues could be considered as a fuel system related factor, but the packet does not directly establish fuel system malfunction beyond the carburetor heat control.
Engine failure from internal damage (connecting rod separation, metal debris in oil system, thermal distress from lack of lubrication) is the central mechanical cause of the forced landing.
Progressive loss of oil pressure, oil pump rotational scoring, and holes in the crankcase point to an engine oil system failure or loss of oil as the initiating fault.
The pilot added 9 quarts of oil the day before, and the small amount of oil found suggests possible fluid loss or inadequate oil quantity, though the cause is unresolved.
Maintenance performed the day before (oil change and oil addition, with the STC engine installation) may have contributed to the oil system fault, but evidence is not conclusive.

findings.label: 02-06-20-maintenance
findings.rationale: placeholder
The crankshaft idler gear disengaged from the crankshaft and camshaft gears, indicating an accessory gear train failure in the engine's gear drive assembly.
Fasteners were not lockwired and torque requirements from Lycoming service instructions were likely not met, indicating a maintenance/inspection deficiency; maintenance records were unavailable.
Engine internal mechanical failure from the idler gear separation damaged the engine's internal drive components, pointing to an engine (reciprocating) mechanical failure.
Engine controls category is a stretch; the failure is mechanical in the accessory/idler gear train, so this is weak support.

Maintenance task performance (failure to properly torque and lockwire the idler shaft fasteners per Service Instruction 1310A) is a plausible personnel contribution, though unverified given missing records.
The right engine throttle control arm was loose from the throttle arm (serrated interface worn), causing loss of commanded thrust on the right engine, which is an engine control failure.
The annual inspection by the director of maintenance failed to detect the loose throttle arm connection with worn serrations, a maintenance/inspection task performance lapse.
During the single-engine emergency the pilots did not use the emergency checklist or feather the failed engine, and the approach/go-around decisions led to a low-altitude loss of control.
The flight school maintenance department was short-staffed and the DOM felt pressure to complete required inspections on time, indicating inadequate resources and scheduling pressure.
The pilot receiving instruction was focused on the emergency and did not check engine gauges, indicating high workload and poor task management during the emergency.

Pilot in IMC with no recent instrument flight experience performed a series of 360° turns and lost control, consistent with spatial disorientation from loss of visual references as described in the packet.
Pilot's instrument currency was lapsed (no instrument flights in 6 months, no IPC in 12 months, simulated-only approaches), indicating insufficient recent instrument experience for IFR operations.
Overcast ceilings around 400-700 ft agl and reduced visibility in mist/fog created IMC conditions that obscured the ground and horizon near the accident site.
Pilot's decision to launch into IMC on a flight with limited instrument proficiency and no weather briefing reflects poor information processing or decision-making about the flight's feasibility.
Pilot appeared to have difficulty understanding and interpreting the GTN 750 and EDM-700 displays, suggesting inadequate use of equipment and information during the approach.
Engine lost all power and postaccident teardown found piston No. 4 seized and unable to move, indicating an internal engine failure.
The reciprocating engine (912S) suffered a power loss with a seized cylinder, pointing to a reciprocating engine internal mechanical failure.
General power plant failure category captures the loss of engine power leading to the forced landing.
The forced landing in a field resulted in a hard landing that fractured the wing, reflecting a possible decision or information-processing issue during the emergency approach.
The weld on the exhaust pipe had multiple cracks and holes with oil and soot in the cracks, indicating exhaust system failure as the accident mechanism.
Maintenance records show a cracked exhaust pipe was repaired and reinstalled in 2021 and the repair left the cracked weld in service, suggesting inadequate maintenance or repair.
Engine exhaust cracking could allow exhaust gas leakage into the cabin, a plausible but unconfirmed pathway given the CO discussion, though the pilot's carboxyhemoglobin was normal.
Cracks in the exhaust pipe weld are a component-level issue, and the fuselage structure is only a remote consideration, so this is weakly supported.
Engine stopped (went silent) shortly after takeoff at 100-150 ft due to piston hole from pre-ignition or lean-mixture overheating, a power plant failure.
Carburetor main jet was changed to leaner setting and non-approved airbox/filter modification altered carburetion, leading to lean mixture and piston damage.
Pilot's response to the simulated and actual loss of power was inadequate, as the instructor had to prompt aggressive nose lowering to maintain airspeed after engine loss on takeoff.
Pilot had very limited experience in this specific motorglider type (one prior flight, minimal self-launch training), indicating insufficient experience for the operation.
Pilot attempted a first solo takeoff in a newly built, minimally tested aircraft with a modified engine configuration, indicating inadequate flight preparation.

Engine lost partial power with no internal failure found, but the power turbine containment ring bolts were missing and the engine was an unapproved gas generator/power section mismatch, pointing to an engine-internal power turbine/engine issue.
The power plant as a whole was configured outside manufacturer instructions (PT6A-15AG gas generator with PT6A-27 power section, unapproved CT vane repair), supporting a power plant-level finding.
Maintenance deficiencies are evident: three containment ring bolts were missing, remaining bolts were not safety wired per the manual, and the engine was mismatched with an unapproved configuration.
Fuel control unit was fractured and could not be bench tested, and oily buildup in the Px air fitting suggests a possible fuel control/metering issue contributing to partial power loss.
Pond water and debris were ingested into the P3 air filter housing and the engine exterior, a possible environmental contributor during the low-level agricultural operation near a pond.
The incident is fundamentally a severe turbulence encounter in convective weather at FL370, with peak EDR 0.62 and 30-degree bank, injuring cabin crew and a passenger.
The turbulence arose from embedded thunderstorms and a squall line with cumulonimbus tops above cruise altitude, so convective weather is the underlying environmental condition.
The crew chose to remain above the cloud tops and turned toward a developing buildup rather than descending or avoiding it earlier, a decision-making factor in penetrating convective cells.
Cabin crew were kept on the floor or in service during turbulence-prone phase before seatbelt securing, possibly relating to training on turbulence procedures, though the evidence is weak.
Engine lost all power shortly after takeoff with no identified mechanical deficiency, pointing to an engine power loss whose root cause is not established by the examination.
The packet does not determine the cause of the engine power loss, so the cause remains undetermined on the available evidence.
Engine fuel and control system is a plausible cause of sudden power loss after takeoff, though the fuel pump and fuel supply tested normally and the left magneto was untested.
Ignition system could explain sudden power loss, but the left magneto could not be tested so ignition failure cannot be excluded.
Flames emerging from the upper engine cowling oil access door and a chemical smell suggest an oil-system leak or fire source in the engine oil system.
Fire originated between the engine and firewall, consistent with an engine-compartment fire source in the powerplant, though the specific failed component is undetermined.
Fuel was shut off after the fire began, so a fuel system leak feeding the fire is plausible but unconfirmed.
General power plant category covers the in-flight engine compartment fire that forced the emergency descent and landing.
